title: 'There was no knife on the scene': Family suing after watchdog clears Ontario officer who killed man at traffic stop
subtitle: The SIU cleared the Peel Regional Police officer who shot Jermaine Carby despite finding that evidence had been tampered with
article: Ontario's police watchdog cleared a Peel Regional Police officer who shot and killed a Brampton, Ont., man during a traffic stop, outraging the victim's family.

Special Investigations Unit director Tony Loparco wrote in a news release that three Peel officers "feared for their lives" when one shot the knife-wielding Jermaine Carby on Sept. 24, 2014. The report said officers told an angry Carby, 33, to "drop the knife" when he advanced towards them.

Loparco wrote that the unnamed officer shot at Carby seven times when Carby refused to stop his advance. Carby was struck once in the chest, left forearm, and back. But the knife was never found at the scene and Loparco admitted evidence was tampered with.
"Where did that knife come from?" La Tanya Grant, Carby's cousin, said. "There was no knife found on the scene. Can we really take that into the investigation?"
Grant said she will be launching a civil lawsuit against the Peel Regional Police before the end of the month.
"I'm not shocked, I'm disappointed in the fact they have enough evidence to charge the officer and they still choose not to."

A 13 cm serrated kitchen knife was submitted to the SIU hours later by a Peel Regional Police sergeant. The sergeant said his officer put the knife in a bag after removing it from Carby's hand as he lay on the ground.

"It is highly regrettable that one officer removed the knife from the scene," Loparco wrote. "His ill-advised conduct has cast a pall over the integrity of the SIU's investigation ... the removal of the knife ensures that some members of the community will harbour concerns, legitimate concerns in my view, regarding the very existence of the knife."
Grant, who has been running the Justice for Jermaine campaign to bring light to her cousin's death and the investigation that has followed, wasn't pleased with the findings.
"Pardon my French, but how much more bullsh-t could the story get?" Grant said to The Canadian Press on Tuesday night.
She hired a private investigator months ago after growing weary of waiting for the SIU's decision.
"If they're not going to do their job, I guess I'll do their job for them," Grant said.
Grant said she's interviewed the witnesses on the scene and most said Carby did not have a knife. One said if he did have a knife, "it had to be very small because he could not see it at all."
Grant hopes to release the evidence she accumulated in her investigation after she receives autopsy and toxicology reports from the coroner.

Loparco also wrote the SIU investigation wasn't thorough because the officer who shot and killed Carby refused to be interviewed for the investigation and didn't submit his notes of the event, as is his legal right.

"While the officer was within his legal rights to choose to remain silent, the SIU is without any direct evidence regarding what is essentially a subjective element of the defence, namely, whether the subject officer believed he was acting to defend himself or his colleagues when he shot Mr. Carby."
A spokesman said Peel Regional Police "agree with the conclusion the officers were justified and lawful in their actions."
All the involved officers are relieved this matter has been finally concluded," Sgt. Matt Small told The Canadian Press in an email Tuesday night, calling it "a tragic event for all involved."
Loparco wrote that, despite his concerns, he was satisfied with the evidence from interviews with six officers and 12 civilian witnesses. He also said that Carby's DNA was present on the knife.
Loparco said Carby was a passenger in a black Volkswagen Jetta that was pulled over by police in Brampton, Ont., because the car's lights weren't on and it had a dangling, obscured licence plate.
The first officer asked Carby for his name and date of birth, and a subsequent database search revealed an outstanding warrant in British Columbia, Loparco said.
The officer then called for backup and waited in his cruiser to approach when other officers arrived, including the one who would end up shooting Carby.

Three officers asked Carby to get out of the car, which he did, the SIU investigation determined. The encounter degenerated into a shouting match that led to Carby advancing on officers with a knife and being shot.

Black Lives Matter-Toronto founder Sandy Hudson said the group will be holding a rally on July 27 for Carby and Andrew Loku, a man who was shot and killed by Toronto police in his apartment building after a dispute with a neighbour led to him confronting her with a hammer.
Hudson said charges should be laid so a fair trial can take place.

"Where's the knife? I think that alone makes it so obvious this case needs to be tried in a court of law," Hudson said. "Everyone should have the right to seek justice through the courts. The facts of this case are suspicious. It just seems really, really fishy. This case reeks."
